extracted.intended_audience: policy-interested general public, policymakers, and regulatory policy wonks
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion piece describing how the Biden administration is reversing Trump-era deregulatory initiatives and explaining the policy tools (executive orders, CRA, judicial appointments, etc.) that shape regulatory trajectories. It is commentary aimed at interpreting regulatory politics and administrative practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-for-one and regulatory budgeting requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An executive order that stipulated each executive agency had to delete two regulations to be permitted to create one new regulation, augmented by a mandate that agencies establish regulatory budgets and tally an annual cost of zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'two for one' and regulatory budgeting scheme requires agencies to price out the benefits and costs of the regulations they issue and keep within spending caps. The op-ed notes regulatory budgeting is used in other nations (e.g., Denmark and Canada), that Trump's order demanded agencies establish regulatory budgets by 2018, and that there were 'conceptual confusions' and implementation problems which hampered its effectiveness. It is presented as a mechanism intended to produce a real and lasting reduction in the corpus of federal regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat guidance as non-binding and create searchable guidance database (Executive Order 13891)
rubrics_metrics.description: An executive order instructing agencies to 'treat guidance documents as non-binding both in law and in practice' and to establish 'a single, searchable, indexed database that contains or links to all guidance documents in effect from such agency or component.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The measure aimed to reduce 'regulatory dark matter'—forms of guidance that have the effect of rules but are not subject to the Administrative Procedure Act (APA)—by increasing transparency and reducing the de facto enforceability of guidance ('Don’t sue anyone for noncompliance'). The op-ed frames this as bringing otherwise hidden agency edicts into the light of day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) coverage limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA of 1946 requires agencies to follow a rulemaking process for formal rules, but it does not extend to various forms of guidance that nonetheless have the effect of rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because guidance often escapes APA's notice-and-comment and publication requirements and sometimes is not made widely available (e.g., 'dear colleague' letters), these instruments raise democratic governance concerns. The op-ed uses this distinction to justify efforts (like Executive Order 13891) to treat guidance as non-binding and improve transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional Review Act (CRA) as a fast-track tool to overturn rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The CRA creates a fast track for legislators to send rule-killing bills to the president’s desk; it was little used since 1996 until revived by GOP legislators during the Trump administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The op-ed cites the GOP sending 'sixteen CRA resolutions' to Trump and notes that Democrats later used the CRA to strike down a Trump rule on methane. The CRA is presented as a procedural lever Congress can use to rapidly nullify recent major regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department of Education grant-selection substantive criteria favoring equity
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed Department of Education regulation that would favor grant applications that fund teaching that 'reflect[s] the diversity, identities, histories, contributions, and experiences of all students [to] create inclusive, supportive, and identity-safe learning environments.' Applicants 'must' show their teaching would 'take into account systemic marginalization, biases, inequities, and discriminatory policy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The op-ed treats this as an example of a substantive rulemaking choice — one that has provoked political outcry — illustrating how agencies use regulatory instruments to shape program priorities and evaluation criteria for grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of executive orders to reverse prior-administration regulatory policies
rubrics_metrics.description: An incoming president can revoke or abolish prior administration's deregulatory mandates by issuing new executive orders — e.g., Biden’s first-day executive order abolishing Trump’s 'two for one,' regulatory budgeting, and regulatory dark matter mandates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes that executive orders are a primary tool for quickly altering the direction of the administrative state, though such reversals may be constrained by law and subsequent enforcement actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial constraints on agency action due to judicial appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: The composition of the federal judiciary affects agencies’ ability to promulgate and defend regulations; the op-ed notes Trump appointed 234 judges, some of whom are skeptical of agencies wielding legislative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial skepticism can produce legal headwinds that block or delay regulatory changes (examples cited include injunctions blocking Biden policies on immigration and evictions). Thus, judicial composition is a structural constraint on administrative rulemaking and reversal efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory output and growth as context for reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical metrics about regulatory activity — e.g., the executive branch finalizes ~4,000 rules each year and proposes another ~2,700; the number of pages of federal regulations grew by 10,000 in Obama’s second term — frame the scale of the administrative state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These quantitative facts are used in the op-ed to justify ambitious deregulatory or regulatory-control mechanisms (like regulatory budgeting) and to emphasize how difficult it is to make a lasting dent in the stock of federal regulations without systemic reforms.
